Overview/RPTL § 581 Rental Comps

Valuation Explainer · NY RPTL § 581

Why NYC values condos using rental comps, not sale prices, on Phase 1 pied-à-terre bills

Two similarly priced condominium sales can have very different assessed market values. New York Real Property Tax Law § 581 uses rental properties as the valuation benchmark.

Look up a condo: Search any unit or BBL on our Live NYC Unit & BBL Pied-à-Terre Checker → to see its FY2027 DOF value (finmkttot) and Phase 1 bracket, or inspect a 2-page Sample Assessment Report PDF ($79).

What RPTL § 581 actually does

Unlike one- to three-family Class 1 homes, which NYC Department of Finance (DOF) values close to recent market sales, Tax Class 2 condominiums and cooperatives are governed by New York Real Property Tax Law § 581. Under § 581, DOF must value the building as though it were a comparable rental apartment building, capitalizing net rental income from selected rental comparables printed on each Notice of Property Value (NOPV), and then apportioning that whole-building figure across units (see also the co-op share guide and building index).

Linking all 968,294 FY2027 roll rows and the July 24 supplemental surcharge roll to 26,317 matched condominium sales and 36,352 Class 1 house sales (Working Paper v2.0), median DOF market values sit at 23.4% of sale price for condos versus 105.5% for houses.

What that rental-proxy distortion produces in Phase 1 (2026–2028)

  • 479 / 1,244 (38.5%)$4M–$6M condominiums whose DOF rental-proxy value reaches the $1,000,000 surcharge cutoff; the other 765 sit below $1M ($0).
  • 39 vs. 0 per 100sampled November 14, 2026 tax statements carrying a surcharge ($48,609 median) at or above $1M vs. below $1M.
  • 77.1%of condo log assessment-ratio variance absorbed by condo declaration fixed effects, showing building-level rental-comp assignments drive the gap.
  • 0.70% → 0.44%inversion in median gross effective surcharge rate across all 26,317 matched condos as sale prices climb from $5–$7.5M to $20M+.

What the records show

Phase 1 uses Class 2 values based on rental comparables through June 2028. The notice of property value identifies the city’s rental comparables. Recorded unit sale prices are a separate measure. The TC107 guide covers the filing rules.
